clips.title: Understanding Dashboards in Grafana | Panels, Visualizations, Queries, and Transformations
clips.why: Grafana's own short tour of what a dashboard and a panel are, before you read one as a JSON file.
look: A dashboard is a set of panels, and each panel is a query plus a way to draw its answer.
The query goes to a data source; Grafana itself stores no metrics.
The same answer can be drawn as a line, a single big number or a table.
clips.after: Our operations dashboard is exactly this: panels whose queries go to VictoriaMetrics, one of them the cache-read share you build in the lab.

clips.title: Provisioning in Grafana | Basics and pitfalls | File examples | Windows and Docker Demo
clips.why: A short demo of provisioning a dashboard from files in a Docker container, which is how our dashboards reach Grafana.
look: Two files work together: a provider file that names a folder on disk, and the dashboard JSON inside that folder.
Grafana reads the folder when it starts and again while it runs, so a changed file appears without a click.
The pitfalls he points out: paths inside the container, and what happens when you edit a provisioned dashboard in the UI.
clips.after: Our dashboards are JSON files in the infrastructure repo, so a dashboard change is a reviewed pull request, not a click someone forgot to tell you about.

clips.title: Prometheus Alertmanager
clips.why: One clear walk from an alerting rule written in PromQL, through Alertmanager's configuration, to a message in Slack.
look: The rule is a PromQL expression with a condition, plus a `for` duration and labels.
The rule only decides that something is wrong; Alertmanager decides who hears about it, using the labels.
The Slack receiver needs a webhook URL and a channel, and that is all Slack needs to know.
clips.after: Our rules are evaluated by vmalert instead of Prometheus, but they are written the same way and go through the same kind of Alertmanager route to #ai-agents-alerts.

practice.q: Which query gives the share of input tokens that each agent read from the prompt cache over the last hour?

options.why: Cache reads per second divided by all input-side tokens per second, both grouped by agent, so each agent gets its own ratio between 0 and 1.

Raw counters are totals since the gateway started, so this ratio describes all history, not the last hour. And without sum by, the label sets on the two sides do not match, so the division returns nothing useful.
That is cache reads per second for all agents together. It is a speed, not a share, and it cannot say which agent lost its cache.

practice.q: The agent dropdown on the dashboard allows several agents and an All option. Finish the label matcher so the query works for all of these choices.
practice.hint: Two characters: the matcher that treats the value as a regular expression.
practice.why: Grafana turns several choices into a regex such as (nova|cifix). Only =~ reads it as a pattern; = would look for an agent literally named (nova|cifix).

practice.q: Nova's prompt cache breaks at 18:00 on Friday. The rule is `share < 0.70` with `for: 2h`. Put what happens in order.
items: The share falls under 0.70 and vmalert marks the rule pending for nova
The share stays under 0.70 at every evaluation for two hours
The rule becomes firing and vmalert sends the alert to Alertmanager
Alertmanager matches the alert's labels to the route for the alerts channel
Someone fixes the prompt, the share goes back up, and a resolved message follows
practice.why: A rule is pending first and fires only when the condition held for the whole `for` duration. Alertmanager, not the rule, decides where the message goes, and a resolved message closes the story.

practice.q: A teammate improves the operations dashboard in the Grafana UI and presses Save. The dashboard is provisioned from a file and the provider has allowUiUpdates: false. What happens?

options.text: The change is saved, and the JSON file in git is updated too
options.why: Grafana never writes back to your files. The file in the repo is the source, and Grafana only reads it.

options.text: Grafana refuses with "Cannot save provisioned dashboard", so the change must go into the JSON file through a pull request
options.why: That is the point of provisioning: every change is a reviewed diff in git, and a bad change is a revert.

options.text: The change is saved and stays until someone deletes it
options.why: Even with allowUiUpdates: true, Grafana overwrites the dashboard from the file the next time it reads the folder.

practice.q: The vmalert page shows AICacheReadShareLow as firing for nova, but nothing appeared in Slack. Where do you look first?

options.text: At the alert in Alertmanager: which receiver did its labels route it to?
options.why: The rule did its job. Routing happens in Alertmanager by labels, and a label with a typo quietly sends the alert to the default receiver.

options.text: At the PromQL expression, because it must be wrong
options.why: The rule is firing, so the expression found the problem. The message got lost after the rule.

options.text: At the Grafana dashboard's refresh interval
options.why: Dashboards and alert rules are separate. A rule fires whether or not anyone has the dashboard open.
